title: I built a multiplayer browser RPG with Claude Code in about 3.5 weeks. Here's how the workflow ended up
author: HanlinBiness
selftext:
Meadowbrook is a shared-world pixel RPG that runs in the browser, desktop and phone. First commit was November 3rd, it's been live since early in the month, and about 490 heroes have been made so far. Play now, no sign-up: [https://meadowbrookrpg.com/?ref=reddit-aigamedev](https://meadowbrookrpg.com/?ref=reddit-aigamedev)

AI disclosure: the code is written with Claude Code. \[How much of the code you wrote or edited yourself.\] Art is drawn in code or made by sprite scripts, no image generators. Spell effects are a CC0 pack by Foozle, and the music is played from CC0 orchestra samples. Design, direction and playtesting are mine.



Rough size, for the curious:

\- Go server with SQLite, about 124k lines (a lot of that is tests)

\- TypeScript client, Phaser for 2D on phones and three.js for the 3D view on desktop

\- 2,100+ commits, 700+ map files, about 3,000 monsters, each with its own pixel sprite stored as text (palette plus rows)

\- Runs on a $7/month Lightsail box



What made it work, more than the model itself:



1. Tools before tasks. Almost 100k lines are tooling: a script that plays a hero from the shell, a screenshot tool, a phone test that runs the same check in Chrome, Safari and Firefox, load tests, balance sims. Once Claude can see and play the game, it can check its own work and doesn't just say it's done.



2. Written rules it has to follow. There's a doc of what each class is for (who has the highest crits, who tanks, who heals), and every balance pass is checked against it. Without that, classes slowly blurred into each other.



3. A voice rule for game text. Left alone, the NPC lines read like AI: every line ending on a punchline, the same jokes copied around. There's a style guide and a small checker script now, and the text is mostly plain.



4. Separate agents for separate jobs. A content agent builds regions and dungeons as data only and never touches code. A test agent maintains tests. Review agents take screenshots and compare against research notes. Each one works in its own git worktree and lands through a merge gate.



5. Measure, don't trust. Every change that touches loading gets a before/after size check. That's how a new player's first download went from about 1 MB to about 700 KB.



What still goes wrong: agents redrawing a sprite another run already made, flaky tests, and big balance passes that need me to say no. \[One thing that surprised you, good or bad.\]



Happy to answer questions about any of it. Feedback on the game is very welcome too, especially on phones.
